utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon with my colleagues, Salvatore Cannata, Carolyn Edgerton, and our case manager, Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. It is Novak Lukic appearing for the accused Perisic with Mr. Guy-Smith and our case managers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness will be called and led by Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can have the witness brought in. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, ma'am. And good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I wonder if you could state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: My name is Sabina Sabanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this witness will give evidence today in respect of a sniping incident, scheduled sniping incident number 8 to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Sabanic, do you remember giving testimony in front of a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal in February of last year, 2007?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, it was in this courtroom, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in preparing for your testimony today, did one of my colleagues read back to you a copy of the transcript of your earlier testimony in 2007 in your own language?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you understood everything you heard?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, also, preparing to testify today, did you have a chance to read copies of the two previous statements you gave to ICTY investigators; one in 1996 and one in 2006?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you also have an opportunity to look at copies of photos that you had marked during the course of your previous testimony here in 2007?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I understand, as a result of the review, you wanted to note for the Trial Chamber, first, three small corrections to the transcript of your evidence in the earlier proceedings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could assist everyone by referring to the specific page and line number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then you could confirm to me, if I understand your corrections accurately. First, on page 1461, line 18, the word "Batika," B-a-t-i-k-a, should be changed to read "Otika." Page 1465, line 14, the words "news station" should be changed to read "next station." And page 1469, line 17, the word "wall" should be changed to read "war." Are those the corrections to the transcript you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I understand also that in respect of a photograph you were shown and marked during your earlier testimony, you wish to make a clarification for this Trial Chamber; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could have that photograph called up, please. It should be 65 ter 07188.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see a photograph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this the photograph that you wish to make a clarification in respect of?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What's the clarification you'd like to make today?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: This is the photograph that had been given to me to show where the fire came from. There are three skyscrapers here on the photo, but in Sarajevo there are four.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the three skyscrapers shown here on the photo, those are the skyscrapers you marked as being representative of the origin of fire in your previous testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could have the witness shown a further photograph, 65 ter number 8600, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see this second photograph on the screen -- on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, based on what you've just said in respect of four skyscrapers and not three, could I ask you this: To your mind, is this an accurate photograph of the area you've described as being the origin of fire of the shot that hit you on 23 November 1994?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have the blank photograph, please, marked as an exhibit, then, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The blank photograph is admitted into evidence as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, although I realise you marked a number of photographs during your previous testimony, I'd like to ask you to take the pen on the right-hand side of the monitor in your hand, and so that we're all clear here today, perhaps you could mark, to the best of your recollection, the location at which you were when you realised -- or, the tram you were riding in was when you realised that you had been shot. And perhaps you could mark it with an X.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your previous testimony, you indicated that you were riding on the tram facing an area you called Grbavica at the moment you were shot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are all of these four skyscrapers in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were all four of these skyscrapers, then, in Bosnian Serb-held territory on 23 November 1994?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, does this photograph and the clarification you've made today change your position in any regard with respect to the origin of fire of the shot that hit you?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: No. I don't change anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, to further clarify, is your position that the shot came from any of the three skyscrapers that you marked earlier in your testimony, or in your previous testimony, or any one of these four skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Any one of these four.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, apart from these corrections and clarifications, if I asked you all the same questions today as you were asked during your previous testimony, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, Your Honours, I would move this photograph, now marked, into evidence and the previous testimony and exhibits marked by this witness in the Dragomir Milosevic case as exhibits, please. May I supply Your Honours with the 65 ter numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 65 ter numbers of what?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The transcript of Mrs. Sabanic's previous testimony, the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll begin with the item I just mentioned; 09295, being the transcript of her previous testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case; 09289, being her ICTY statement from 1995; 09290, being her ICTY statement from 2006; 092, pardon me, 92, being a photograph; 07187, being a photograph; 07188, which was the photograph that she referred to originally now in her testimony; 09293 and 09294, being the last two photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Edgerton. I've lost you at some stage when you said "pardon me." I didn't think -- I don't think you finished the 0 -- the 65 ter number that you were pronouncing. Was it 92 -- 092 what?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just look at my transcript, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 09292. And that was a photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. So it goes 9295, being the transcript of her testimony; 9289; 90; and 92; and then we move to 7187, 7188, 9293, and 9294.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All those 65 ter numbers -- exhibits with those numbers are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number, or exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The marked photograph 08600 will be Exhibit P101, Your Honours. 65 ter 09295 will be Exhibit P102. 65 ter 09289 will be Exhibit P103, Your Honours. 65 ter 09290 will become Exhibit P104. 65 ter 09292 will be Exhibit P105, Your Honours. 65 ter 07187 will be Exhibit P106. 65 ter 07188 will become Exhibit P107. 65 ter 09293 will be Exhibit P108. And 65 ter 09294 will be Exhibit P109, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Registrar, if you might, just for my own edification, what was Exhibit P100?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That was the unmarked photographed 08600, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph on the screen before it was marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. And I thought you said now 8600 is P101? Have we not duplicated something there? When you started now, you said 8600 is P101.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The unmarked 8600 is P100, Your Honour; the marked 8600 is P101. Especially in -- when we're in e-court, I think it's useful to have an unmarked photograph in there for later purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But she never marked the previous photograph in this courtroom. The previous photograph which had three skyscrapers had markings from a previous testimony, and she never marked it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct. And I only tendered that one as part of her 92 ter package. That was 7188. The previous photograph with the three skyscrapers marked during the Dragomir Milosevic testimony was 7188. The unmarked photograph with four skyscrapers, the full-on view, was 8600, which we've now marked as P100. The marked full-on four skyscrapers with the X --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We may proceed. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours, as has been the practice, I would now like to read a very short summary of the evidence that's now been admitted, Mrs. Sabanic's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At about 4 p.m. on 23 November 1994, the witness was riding a crowded tram in Sarajevo, standing facing the Serb army-held area of Grbavica when she was injured by sniper-fire coming from skyscrapers in Grbavica. Shots were always coming from there. The tram is filled with civilians, mostly women. It had been a peaceful, clear day. The trams didn't run every day, only on the days during cease-fires when there was no shooting. The witness saw no soldiers in the area at the time she was shot, nor any combat between the two armies. That being concluded, nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Sabanic, good morning. My name is Novak Lukic, and I appear for the Defence team of Momcilo Perisic. I will ask you a few questions. You have experience here in the Tribunal. You know that when we speak the same language, you have to make a slight pause after each of my questions so that interpreters can keep up and that we don't overlap. Mrs. Sabanic, throughout the war you lived in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said in your testimony and in your statement that this incident happened when you were going to work, or, rather, when you were coming home from work. Did you work throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I started to work in September 1994 and from then onwards, because of using sick-leave after the incident, I missed some time. But normally I continued to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In fact, this incident happened about two months after you started working.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From what I understood, your job was somewhere in the centre of town. Could you tell us more precisely where you worked? I don't need the address, but ...

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I worked in Titova Street, near the eternal flame monument.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your second statement given to the OTP you stated in paragraph 6, in rather great detail, that on several occasions during the war in Sarajevo you changed your place of residence. I'll go through it very quickly and you'll just confirm if it's correct. You said that before the war you lived in Dobrinja neighbourhood. Then you moved to Fojnica. That's probably when the war started; correct?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was March/April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you returned to Sarajevo, and then you lived in Kosevo for a while; correct?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: On Kosevo hill, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you lived in Skerliceva Street, probably until September 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I believe I moved to Skerliceva in June 1994, maybe July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you moved to Buca Potok, and you said the living conditions were better there but it was more difficult to get to work, and that was at the time when you were wounded you lived in that location.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you move to this street, Cobanija?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were probably aware, Mrs. Sabanic - you changed addresses very often - you were probably aware that there were a lot of abandoned apartments in Sarajevo during the war.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were also probably aware that there were many abandoned apartments formerly belonging to JNA officers and JNA personnel and civil servants who had left Sarajevo before the war.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: All I can say is that I never used any of these apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was: Had you heard that there were such abandoned apartments?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during the war, what was the source of your information about events and developments in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that we had electricity, we could get information from the news bulletin on the TV in the evening and from all the other media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you were unable to watch or listen to the media, I assume you received information from the people around you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: There were also newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They were published in Sarajevo, and you were able to get newspapers regularly and get information from those?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes. The newspaper Oslobodjenje came out regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll put a few general questions to you to see whether you have any knowledge concerning these issues. In your environment, did you have anyone who was actively involved in the military structures of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, either at work, among our colleagues, or in your family, among your neighbours, your extended family, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by "military structures," please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, a person who was a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear or were you aware that both sides, and when I say "both sides," I mean the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had sniper weapons and mortars?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I was a civilian and what I experienced on my own skin I know came from the Serbian side. They were shooting at our civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But my question was very precise. We'll come to the incident. My simple question was: Were you aware that both sides, to be precise the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, also had snipers and mortars? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Sarajevo, in the course of the conflict, was a divided city; that the river Miljacka divided two territories, one side controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were able to get information from the media and from people you knew were in the BH Army, so did you know that there were between 30 and 40.000 members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that between 1994 and 1995, in that period, a considerable quantity of weapons were delivered to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from outside and that that army became much better armed and better equipped?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that both sides, and by that I mean the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Army of Republika Srpska, violated the cease-fires in the course of the war and that both sides were cautioned by UNPROFOR for that reason?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I know only about one side and that's the Serbian side, because I experienced it myself. I felt it on my own skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina violated cease-fires? You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said in your statements and in your testimony in the Milosevic case, and you also confirmed today, that it was common knowledge in Sarajevo that these three or four skyscrapers were positions from which members of the Army of Republika Srpska fired sniper shots; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that this line of fire passed through the buildings of two museums and that this was the most dangerous part of the route you took, and that after that it was a little safer. Did I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Milosevic case, Dragomir Milosevic, on page 1469 -- sorry, no, I was right, 1469, you stated that you had never held a weapon in your hands. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And on the same page, when asked by Their Honours, you said you didn't know from what position it was easier to fire for the person doing the firing.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you give us a reference for that, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 1469, from line 15 to line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Sabanic, in the course of your testimony, when expressly asked by Their Honours, you stated that you assumed the shot was fired from those skyscrapers because that was the side the bullets came from, and in your view it was common knowledge that these were sniper nests, so to speak, on those skyscrapers held by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat her answer? It was very feint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please excuse me for the intervention. The interpreters are having a bit of trouble hearing Mrs. Sabanic, I think because you're leaning a bit back in the chair, and they asked her to repeat the last answer because it wasn't interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your last answer, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what I asked you?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That you stated at the time that you assumed that the shots came from that direction because it was common knowledge that snipers were firing from that location. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were also positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on that side, before the river Miljacka?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you, Mr. Lukic. Your question at line 18, you say that "You stated at the time that you assumed that the shots came from that direction because it was common knowledge that snipers were firing from that location." When you say "stated at that time," are you talking about -- are you referring to the Milosevic testimony, or what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to both. I put to the witness what she stated during her testimony in the Milosevic case, at that time, but in that testimony she stated that at the time of the incident it was common knowledge that that was a location where there were Serb forces who were opening sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you please give us the reference in the Milosevic transcript where that has been said, where the assumption has been mentioned and where the common knowledge has been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Excuse me. Judge Robinson put his question ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If it assists at all, I can find two page references, but I don't see the word "assumed" anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps my friend could look at page 1454 and the continuation of the answer at 1455.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Please excuse me for a moment. Page 1475. Just a moment. Page 1475 and 1476.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line reference at 1475?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From line 9 to the end of the page and then at the top of page 1476.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic, to say "from line 9 to the end of the page," I just want to see the line where the words "assumed" and "common knowledge" are found. Just give me the specific line, because now we're wasting time reading the whole page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wish to waste time either, Your Honours. I put my question in the way I did, but I think that the witness's reply is in the same -- is to the same effect, and I think that even the Prosecution stated that in their summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, you're going to have to give me where they say so in their summary. I'm afraid, Mr. Lukic, if you are not able to refer us to any reference, I'll ask you to rephrase those questions. The statement of common knowledge and assumption, if you cannot give us any reference, would have to be expunged. You would have to rephrase that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can put the question without referring to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it common knowledge in Sarajevo at the time that shots were fired from those skyscrapers by members of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: That stretch of road where I was wounded was the riskiest, the most dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what you were aware of as a passenger on that tram running on that line, is that people said or you heard from the media that members of the Army of Republika Srpska were firing sniper shots in that direction; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just people saying that. It was that there was the largest number of people who were wounded. People who were wounded were mostly wounded on that stretch of road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in connection with those incidents, the information that was given out was always --

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, because that was the place where people were killed or wounded most often, on that stretch of road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You certainly knew that there were also highrise buildings in areas controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you stated that when answering questions in the last testimony you gave at this trial, the Energoinvest building, the Unis building, the Marsal Tito barracks, the museums, and so on; is that right? They were on the territory controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: In the course of my last testimony, I was given pictures where I was supposed to indicate those buildings, the museums, the buildings at Pofalici. I didn't know why I had to indicate them. I only had to indicate them and mark them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the buildings I have just mentioned, they were on the territory held --

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were on the other side of the Miljacka, on the other bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that the area of Grbavica was also shelled and that sniper shots were fired also in that period but from the other side? Did you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: No, we did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to discuss the incident itself, then. A moment ago you were drawing a picture, and I suppose the Trial Chamber understands you were going from town, from the centre of town, and the Miljacka river was on your right.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: No, it was opposite me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right, opposite. You said it was the last run of the tram for that day. The tram stopped working at 4 p.m. I need an answer. A nod of the head is not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how long had you been in the tram from the time when you got into the tram until the moment you were wounded? How many stops, let's say, or minutes?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you how many minutes because it was the last tram for the day. You can never say exactly how many passengers are getting on and off. It took longer perhaps than a tram would normally take today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we, in the courtroom, we don't know how long it takes from the centre of town to the Marsal Tito barracks. When you got in, was the tram already full? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was packed, because that stop was -- the tram goes in a circular line in Sarajevo, so people get in at any stop. Some people use the tram just to go one stop further so that they wouldn't walk because it was dangerous. And it probably ran twice as slowly as it does today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said the tram was packed. Were you able to move through the tram, or did you have to stop at the end of the car where you got in? And that's something I seem to have read in your statement.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I couldn't move through the tram. As I got in through the door, I stopped there. I didn't move from one section of the tram to another. It was really very crowded and you couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you said in your statement that there were no members of the army in the tram, and I suppose you can't say that with a hundred per cent certainty because you were not able to move through the crowded tram. You could see there were no members of the BH army around you, but you couldn't say that there weren't any in the tram, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes. But when we stopped, we all had to get out, so I could see all the people who had been on that tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the criminal report it says that there were around 200 people in the tram.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that, but there were many of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 1476 of your testimony, you said you hadn't heard a shot; you just felt pain at that moment.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also stated on page 1454 that you suppose the shot had come from one of those three skyscrapers that you called "shopping" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1454. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What line?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question of the Chamber is line 24 and the answer is in line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my case it wasn't from the shopping buildings. It's a bit further at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in one statement that it was that area that fire came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question at line -- page 20, line 23, says that "at page 1454 of the transcript" the witness "supposed the shot had come from one of those three skyscrapers that you called 'shopping,'" and, in fact, she makes no reference to that name for the skyscrapers in those pages of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be precise, Your Honours. Her first statement, which is now Exhibit P103, paragraph 10, I quote from the B/C/S version: "I knew that on the tram line there were places that were more dangerous than others because there had been other cases of sniping on the trams." In B/C/S -- sorry. "On the Serb side of the conflict line in Grbavica, in the neighbourhood we called 'shopping,' there are three skyscrapers. This is a place from which fire can be opened on the trams."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Sabanic, let me ask you this: At any point after this incident and before your testimony and before or after giving a statement to the OTP, had you been in contact with any person from the Agency for Investigation and Documentation or the Security Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: You mean after the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I mean before.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I didn't directly talk to anyone after the -- about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And why did they contact you, if I may know?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: They contacted me once to take me to Nedzarici so that I could give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose the OTP office was in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion before your testimony in the Milosevic case to be shown the criminal report and the record of that incident, the police record?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which incident are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean now the incident where the witness was wounded on the 23rd of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Buco Kemal mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How about the name Hafiza Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when the OTP interviewed you the first or the second time, because there were two interviews and also the proofing in the Milosevic case, did anyone from the OTP show you any kind of document, any kind of official document, related to this incident so that you can give your comments? I mean the incident when you were wounded. Apart from sketches and photographs. That is not of interest to me.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Nothing apart from my statements that I was asked to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, which is now P103, you stated in paragraph 4 - and that's how it is recorded in the statement - I quote: "The first thing I heard was the glass shattering." That was recorded in the statement. And at the trial in the Milosevic case you said that was not properly recorded, that you, in fact, had not heard the glass shattering. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: After I gave a statement and after the first reading back of the statement to me, I immediately corrected that. I said I never heard the glass being smashed, and it must be some sort of error that keeps dragging on from the very beginning. But I had corrected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you correct it?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: When I was asked to sign the statement after I first gave it, I stated plainly that, in fact, I hadn't heard the glass being smashed or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were giving your second statement, which is now Exhibit P104, a statement given on the 22nd of May, 2006, your original statement was shown to you, and it still contained the phrase I just read. You made certain corrections to paragraph 2 of that statement, but you had no comment on the paragraph 4. It continued to read: "The first thing I heard was the glass being smashed." Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: My comment on that is that, since I said the first time it needs to be corrected, it was superfluous to say anything further about that glass because I said when giving the first statement that, in fact, I hadn't heard any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell on this too much, but after so many years you saw that sentence still there and you didn't ask for it to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: In the Milosevic trial there was also discussion about that glass and I said once again that I hadn't heard anything and that I had corrected the first statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 1484 of the Milosevic transcript, you said that once in the hospital you heard another man had been killed in that incident. Do you remember what you said and how it was recorded? If I tell you now that the Office of the Prosecutor, in its indictment, does not mention any other deaths in the incident, would you say that the information you received was inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: The lady who lay with me in the same room, in the same ward, had been on the same tram with her husband, and her husband was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you know that the lady next to you was injured?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. And in conclusion I will have just one more question. You said in your first statement given back in November 1995, paragraph 9, you said: "I won't take the tram anymore until peace it restored." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember saying that, but it seems to me a normal reaction at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read it back to you. I quote: "From that day on I'll no longer ride the tram as long as the peace is not restored." When did that occur, in fact?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I think we felt safer only after the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's September 1996.

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one question, again to be absolutely clear on something.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Sabanic, at page 21, line 11, of the transcript of the testimony today, you referred to other locations, and I'll quote exactly, you referred -- you stated that "on the tram line, there were places that were more dangerous than others because there had been other cases of sniping on trams." Sorry, I'm quoting Mr. Lukic now, pardon me. "In the neighbourhood we called 'shopping,' there are three skyscrapers. This is a place from which fire can be opened on the trams." Just to be absolutely clear, are those four buildings you identified as the source of the gun-fire from which you were injured the development called "shopping"?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: There's four buildings, but the "shopping" project is a bit further away. But in our colloquial exchanges, everyday exchanges, we used the name "shopping" to refer to that entire area of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In -- is the physical appearance of the development called "shopping" different in any way from the four skyscrapers you identified as being the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: "Shopping" has three skyscrapers, and the other development has four.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What colour are the skyscrapers of the "shopping" development?

utterances.speaker: SABINA SABANIC
utterances.text: I think -- I really can't remember now. I think they are yellow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Edgerton. Judge? Judge, questions? Any questions for the witness? Thank you. Thank you, ma'am. That brings us to the end of your testimony. On behalf of the Tribunal, I want just to say thank you for coming and taking time to come and testify. You are now excused and you may stand down. And please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Cannata will call the next witness, but I note the time. Would this be the proper time for the first break, or would you rather have the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've got about 4 minutes to go before the break is due. Mr. Cannata, would you rather we took the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you can give me a couple of minutes to switch the work station with my colleague Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome to do that. Please do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you now better able to answer my question, Mr. Cannata? Okay. You proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, it took a little bit longer than you expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I asked the question, would you rather we took the break now or -- oh, I realise you want to proceed, but we've got now 2 minutes to go before break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Okay. My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. We'll swear the witness, and we'll have to take the break after that, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Actually, I had an issue to raise before the witness was to be brought here, but I can actually do it now. Madam Witness has some difficulties in reading and writing. I would therefore ask permission by Your Honours to have the declaration read out to her, if it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It won't be a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please read the declaration to the witness and then having read -- first of all, ask her whether she accepts that. I know you don't read B/C/S. Maybe if you read it in English and we can ask the interpreters to interpret it for the witness. THE USHER: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare. THE USHER: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth. THE USHER: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth. THE USHER: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am. You may be seated. Thank you so much. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What do you want to do, Mr. Cannata?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Shall we go for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I think we must apologise to the witness for bringing her in just to take her out again. Our apologies, ma'am. It is time for a break. We'll take a break and come back at a quarter to 11.00 when we'll resume. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Witness Dervisa Selmanovic. Your Honour, this is a 92 ter witness, so we'll go through the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Witness. How do you feel today?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Madam Witness, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Dervisa Selmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Witness, I do understand that you have some difficulties in reading and writing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: But I guess -- I take it that you can write your signature, or at least the initials of your full name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can write my first and last name. I know how to do that. It's not really done very well, but there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: That should be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter 9296 on the e-court, please, the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you see a document in front of you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can you see your full name, your signature, at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you remember that -- whether yesterday this document was read out to you in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, do you confirm that what you say in this document is true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's all true and correct, what I said. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: You will give the same answers, you will say the same things today if asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same. I would answer in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we have this document entered into evidence, it's 65 ter 9296, the first statement by Madam Dervisa Selmanovic, dated 27 February 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 9296 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can I have please have 65 ter 9297 on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you see a document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me. It should be there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: At the top -- at the bottom of the page, do you see your signature?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this document was read back to you yesterday in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, do you confirm that this document -- that what you say in this document is true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's true and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And also that you will give the same answers today if asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would give the same answers today, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I have 65 ter 9297 moved into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P111, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you remember that you testified before in this Tribunal in a different case?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And you testified in the case, the Prosecution versus Dragomir Milosevic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Was a copy -- a copy of the transcripts of your testimony in the case, Prosecution versus -- Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic, read out to you yesterday in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Did you also have an opportunity to review the exhibits associated with that document, that is, the photograph and the video that you would have viewed yesterday? Did you review it?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: They read it to me, what was in there, and what they asked me about I testified to. And I read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you confirm that what you said in the Prosecutor -- in the case against Dragomir Milosevic was true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was true and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Would you give the same answers today if asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would give the same answers today I gave then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Madam Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to move into evidence the transcripts and associated exhibits of Madam Selmanovic's previous testimony in the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic case. I will provide you with the 65 ter numbers; that is, 9299 is the transcript; 8615, 1-5, is the photo, the 360 panoramic photo attached to the transcript; and lastly, 65 ter 4333 is the video concerning this witness incident at the timing 00:42:17 to 00:43:16. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those 65 ter documents are admitted into evidence. May they please be given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 09299 will be Exhibit P112. 65 ter 08615 will be Exhibit P113. And 65 ter 04333 will be Exhibit P114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, at this stage I will read a short summary of Witness Selmanovic's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness Dervisa Selmanovic has given evidence in respect of scheduled incident B9 of the indictment, that is, the incident that occurred on 10 December 1994, when Witness Selmanovic was shot and injured while collecting firewood in the backyard of a house located in Sedrenik Street number 56 in the north-east of Sarajevo. The witness testified that the shots came from Spicaste Stijena as held by the SRK, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. The witness received wounds on her right knee and was treated at the orthopedic clinic of the Medical Centre of the University of Sarajevo. The witness testified that there were no military position anywhere near the area where she was shot. She did not notice any fighting or military activity or military personnel at the time and in the vicinity of the area she was shot. This concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I did not wish to interrupt my learned friend, but I have an objection in principle. When statements -- when the statements were shown to the witness, the Prosecutor said, Would you confirm all the questions and answers in the statement, but we see only answers in the statement, not the questions. I assume that's a mistake, so I just wanted to mention that. The questions are there only on the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Selmanovic, good morning. My name is Novak Lukic, and I appear on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Perisic. I will put some questions to you on his behalf. Do you remember that in connection with the incident that took place on the 10th of December, 1994, as mentioned in the indictment, you gave your first statement concerning this incident to the police in Sarajevo, to Inspector Djozo Nedzib in March 1995, on the 12th of March, 1995, that is.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, since you stated that immediately after you were wounded you were released from hospital and sent home practically on the same day, did anyone from the police visit you from the time you were wounded to the time you made this first statement?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that now because it was a long time ago. A lot of years have passed since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say that I would kindly ask the Chamber to direct my learned friend to give reference to passages of statements and transcripts when quoted, and I refer back to you at page 35, line 1, when the Defence asked, "... since you stated that immediately after ..." and then goes on. I would like to have a reference for that quote of the witness's evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness mentioned this in more than one place in her statement, but just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam, were you released from hospital on the same day, after the incident?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they released me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honours, and then I'll come to that in order to avoid wasting time. The witness has replied now to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. But whenever you put a previous statement by the witness to her, we would like you to give a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour, I understand. I will adhere strictly to your instructions in future when I put anything to a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. But do come back to this one that the Prosecutor has raised, an issue here that he would like to get --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour, yes. I will, certainly. I think I will come to the reference as I proceed with my questions, but if I don't, I will certainly come back to it at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You gave your first statement to the OTP on the 27th of February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you told them at the time or, rather, you attached the record of the statement made at the police station on the 12th of March, 1995. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you made your second statement, the one you gave to the investigators of the OTP, your second statement to the OTP was given in April 1996, and you were given the opportunity of reading all your previous statements, the previous statement given to the Prosecution and the one given to the police. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a lot of time has gone by since then, and I can't remember everything now, you know. I'll tell you everything I can remember. What I can't, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Certainly. But let me jog your memory. In your statement given in 2006, in paragraph 3 it says: "Earlier, previously, I gave a brief statement to the investigator of the ICTY. I have now been shown a copy of that statement made on the 27th of February, 1996. I confirm that this is a correctly recorded statement which I gave to the investigator on the 21st of February, 1996."

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me finish, please. It says: "I was also shown a copy of the statement I gave to the MUP officers on the 12th of March, 1995, and I have read that statement."

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "The statement I made on the 12th of March, 1995, is also correctly recorded; however, the date and place of birth are incorrect." So that was the only correction you made.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also, and this has been admitted into evidence here, met the Prosecution team sometime in the summer of 2006, when there was a reconstruction of the event, and you were filmed using a camera in front of the place where you were hit. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you testified in the Milosevic case, you were shown all these statements and you confirmed that they were accurate, as you have done today.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. You worked for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a cook.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: An assistant cook. I assisted the cook.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please just make a brief pause after my question for the sake of interpretation, to avoid any problems in the transcript. Could you tell us where your place of work was? You said it was at Kosevo.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Behind the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the rest of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness -- the interpreters did not understand the rest of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain more clearly where the place was where you worked at Kosevo.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's behind the skyscraper, right under the sky -- underneath the skyscraper, next to the stadium. That's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any civilians living there? Did people live there?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was a skyscraper and just a road in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what military facilities were there? What was the army doing there? Who was there from the army?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the young men defending the front line. What do I know? I don't know. We took care of the kitchen. I didn't look at anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you said -- I don't want to omit the reference again. But you were advised to take your uniform off when you went home, so you didn't take your uniform away from your place of work.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a uniform, but I never wore it, actually. They gave it to me, but I never wore it. I just wore my civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard people say that there were snipers all around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And yes, there were, because whenever I was going to work, I was always afraid, from Poljo, from Trebevic, from everywhere we were afraid because it came from all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, can I have references for the last two questions, that is, the question at page 38, line -- I'm sorry, line 22, and the next question was at -- well, it was not a question but a statement, but it was page 39, line 2. The references would be very much appreciated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just asked the question deliberately not making a reference, and that's what I said, for the record. I did not refer to any specific part of the witness's testimony. I don't think I'm obliged to constantly give references in my cross-examination. I'm just putting questions that the witness is forced to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cannata, I see you want to stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Well, if the Defence is putting previous evidence to the witness by way of using the expression "and you said," meaning the witness, then it would be, I would consider, wise and advisable to have reference to where the witness was supposedly saying what the Defence is putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, at page 38, line 22, you said, "and you said -- and I don't want to omit the reference again. But you were advised to take your uniform off when you went home, so you didn't take your uniform away from your place of work." Now, I did indicate a little earlier this morning that when you do make references to either statements by the witness or to her testimony in the previous cases, please give the reference. And here you specifically said you don't want to admit to the reference again. Your learned friend on the prosecution side would like you to give the reference, and I would like you to please give the reference, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will then need some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then again at page 39, line 2, you say: "You heard people say that there were snipers all around Sarajevo." Again, if you can give your learned friend where you get that statement from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Transcript page 1603. Let me just find it. Page 1603, line 19, is the reference to the uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, page 1603 of the transcript, at line 19, it reads: "In your opinion, Witness, were there a lot of people working for the BiH army but who did not wear their uniform for the same reasons?" That's what I read there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That includes women. Women also worked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. We understand, madam. If you can just hold on, we're still talking about the lawyer who's asking you questions. You'll answer in a few minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 12. I apologise, Your Honour. The question was in line 12, and the answer is in line 17, on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again, what is being said at those lines, Mr. Lukic, there's no reference to her leaving the uniform at work when she goes home, which is what you are putting to her. Now, the whole purpose, the whole purpose of giving a reference is to ensure that we don't embellish the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe my question into English might have been misinterpreted. My question was not that the uniform was left at work. My question was, in fact, that she did not wear a uniform outside her workplace, but I will make the question clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That didn't come out like that, Mr. Lukic. If you want it read to you, what was translated to the -- on the transcript, it says -- this is, again, page 38, line 22: "And you said -- and I don't want to omit the reference again. But you were advised to take your uniform off when you went home, so you didn't take your uniform away from your place of work." That's how it's translated, and that's what we go by. Now you say you're misinterpreted. Thank you so much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether the army where you were an assistant cook had any snipers?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I didn't know anything about that. All I did was work in the kitchen. I didn't deal with anything else. I just went in and out of the kitchen. I had no other business. I peeled potatoes, prepared rice, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's all I asked you. When I ask a brief question, you can answer very briefly. You were aware, though, that the separation line, the conflict line, was 200 metres away from the place you worked, approximately. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: What do I know? We just took cover when there was gun-fire. I did not dare look around. I just ran to the nearest shelter when there was gun-fire so as to avoid bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know where the separation line was at Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: At Sedrenik, I didn't measure it. I didn't -- well, it was close by. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just give me an answer. That line was approximately 200 metres from the place where you were hit. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at least as the crow flies, 200 metres it was from Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina held the hill called Grdonja?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just told you that I don't know anything about which army was where. All I know is that there was Spicaste Stijena. I knew approximately where our troops were and approximately where the other side's troops were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 1594 in the Milosevic trial, you answered one question this way. I'll read it in English. [In English] "Grdonja is the hill in the right by Grdonj 200 or 300 metres is Spicaste Stijena." [Interpretation] Do you remember stating this in evidence?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you will agree that at the time when you stated that you thought that was the distance between the two places.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember saying that and that's, I believe, how it was. That was the distance as the crow flies between Spicaste Stijena and the place where I was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the BH army members fired from Grdonja and from their own positions they held there at the distance you stated?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's too much to ask of me. I don't know that. All I know is that the shot that hit me came from Spicaste Stijena. How they were opening fire, what they were doing, I really can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me refresh your memory. When you were asked at that Milosevic trial, on page 1603, the question was: "What was the first time you heard that there was gun-fire around Spicaste Stijena?" And you said, in line 5: [In English] "Well, I'm telling you what I know. I know they said, 'They're firing from Spicaste Stijena. Watch out. Take care. They're firing.'"

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] "That's when I learned from Spicaste Stijena. I hadn't known about it until this happened." [Interpretation] My question is: Did you know that gun-fire was coming from Spicaste Stijena before you were hit?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard before that people were saying, Look out, there is fire coming from Spicaste Stijena. It's not like that place was completely unfamiliar to me. I had family there even before the war, and I lived close by during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did you know fire was coming from there when you came to live there?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the fire came from there, sniper fire and other fire. We, who lived there, were targeted the most often.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please try to understand my question. I'm trying to be as precise as I can. Had you heard that gun-fire was coming from that location you mentioned, Spicaste Stijena, only when you came to live in Sedrenik during the war?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard then people saying, Gun-fire is coming from Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You lived in Sedrenik for a number of months; correct?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how long. Perhaps it was as long as a year. I was put up there as a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read it back to you to refresh your memory. Just a moment. Your statement of the 20th April 2006, it is now Exhibit Number P111, paragraph 6, you said, quote: "In May 1994 I found a job as assistant cook in the BH army. The army provided me with a small apartment in the street of Zaima Sarca, in which I reside to date." And in paragraph 5, I quote: "Eventually I found a small house in Sedrenik, and that's where I lived for a few months."

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know for how long, but I did live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But at the time when you were injured, you were not living there?

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Zaima Sarca Street, but the wood that I needed for fuel was still back there in my previous residence, and I had to collect it to take it to my new apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I want to clarify, because in your statement it seems that the OTP, in fact, said that you were living there when you were shot, and from all your other statements it transpires that at the time you were already living in Zaima Sarca Street.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in both places practically at the same time. I had to go back to my previous residence in emergencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please try to remember that. I don't want to push you. But on the day when the incident happened, from the apartment where you had moved in, you went back to your previous residence to get firewood.

utterances.speaker: DERVISA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't remember that precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an issue here. It's page 45, line 8, and I quote: "Because in your statement it seems that the OTP, in fact, said that you were living there ..." Can I ask you for a reference for that statement -- that proposition by the Defence? Instead, it's not -- in the indictment, it's not alleged that Witness Selmanovic was living in the apartment -- in house in Sedrenik Street number 56 where she was shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not mention the indictment at all, Your Honours. I heard today from my learned friend the Prosecutor, when he was reading the summary, that she was injured outside her place of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was read out today was that the incident occurred on the 10th of December, 1994, when Witness Selmanovic was shot and injured while collecting firewood in the backyard of a house located in Sedrenik Street, number 56, in the north-east of Sarajevo. There's no reference to her -- that place being her residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had really understood the Prosecutor as saying that this was her house, her place of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor read out that summary, he read out from a piece of paper and I have the piece of paper here, and I'm reading exactly what I thought he read at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
